record.original_question: How can the long-standing discrepancy between spectroscopic factors extracted from low-energy exclusive (e,e′p) measurements and spectroscopic factors predicted by nuclear many-body theory be resolved in a reaction framework that consistently includes final-state interactions, current-operator ambiguities, and relativistic effects? In particular, can one explain why low-Q² analyses report strongly quenched valence-shell strengths while higher-Q² analyses give substantially larger values, without attributing the difference to uncontrolled model dependence in the reaction mechanism?

evidence.quote: However, model calculations produce spectroscopic factors Sα much larger than those extracted in low-energy (e,e′p) data.

A possible Q2-dependence of spectroscopic factors, jumping from values around 0.6–0.7 at low Q2 to unity at Q2 ≥ 1 GeV2, simply means that something is not under control in either experiment or theory or both.

A striking feature coming out of the present analysis of (e,e′p) world data is an apparent Q2 dependence of the extracted spectroscopic factors. This is clearly not acceptable and indicates that something is missing in the theoretical treatment of the reaction mechanism.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider exclusive quasi-elastic electron-induced single-proton knockout reactions $A(e,e'p)B$, in which a high-energy electron scatters off a nucleus $A$ with four-momentum transfer $q^\mu=(\omega,\mathbf{q})$ and $Q^2=-q^\mu q_\mu$, ejecting a proton while leaving the residual nucleus $B$ in a definite (typically valence) bound state $\alpha$. Within a one-body current picture, the cross section is proportional to the squared overlap between the initial state of $A$ and the final state $|B,\alpha\rangle\otimes|p\rangle$. The normalization of this overlap defines the spectroscopic factor $S_\alpha\in[0,1]$, which many-body nuclear structure calculations (including short-range and long-range correlations) typically predict to lie near $S_\alpha^{\text{th}}\approx 0.7$–$0.9$ for valence orbitals of stable nuclei.

Experimental extractions of $S_\alpha$ from such $(e,e'p)$ data require a reaction model that accounts for: (i) final-state interactions between the outgoing proton and the residual nucleus (usually treated through a complex optical potential in a distorted-wave framework), (ii) ambiguities in the off-shell electromagnetic single-nucleon current operator (different prescriptions such as $CC1$, $CC2$, $CC3$), and (iii) relativistic kinematic and dynamical effects in the bound-state wave function, the current, and the distorted outgoing wave.

Empirically, analyses of low-$Q^2$ exclusive $(e,e'p)$ data (with $Q^2$ well below $1\,\text{GeV}^2$) yield strongly quenched valence-shell spectroscopic factors $S_\alpha^{\text{exp}}\approx 0.6$–$0.7$ of the independent-particle-shell-model value, whereas analyses performed at $Q^2\gtrsim 1\,\text{GeV}^2$ yield $S_\alpha^{\text{exp}}$ close to unity using analogous reaction frameworks.

Problem. Construct a single, internally consistent reaction-theoretical framework for $A(e,e'p)B$ that simultaneously incorporates final-state interactions, off-shell single-nucleon current ambiguities, and relativistic effects, in which the extracted valence-shell spectroscopic factors $S_\alpha$ become independent of $Q^2$ across the kinematic range from a few hundred $\text{MeV}^2$ up to several $\text{GeV}^2$, and either reconcile the resulting $Q^2$-independent values with the predictions of modern nuclear many-body theory or identify, within that consistent framework, the specific physical ingredient whose omission produces the observed apparent $Q^2$ dependence. In particular, account for the difference between low-$Q^2$ quenched values and high-$Q^2$ near-unity values without invoking uncontrolled model dependence of the reaction mechanism.
artifact.status_search_result: The discrepancy between spectroscopic factors extracted from $(e,e'p)$ at different $Q^2$ and many-body predictions remains an active and unresolved puzzle in nuclear physics. Recent work (e.g., Phys. Rev. Lett. 131, 212503 (2023) and follow-ups, plus a 2025 explanation proposing a core-screening / finite-probe-size effect) provides partial reconciliations and Bayesian uncertainty quantification, but no universally accepted, fully consistent reaction framework removes the apparent $Q^2$ dependence and matches many-body theory across the full kinematic range. Hence the problem is best described as partially solved.

status_evidence.title: New Perspectives on Spectroscopic Factor Quenching from Reactions
status_evidence.snippet: First consistent analysis of one-nucleon transfer and knockout data with Bayesian uncertainty quantification of reaction-model inputs.
status_evidence.claim: Recent work provides a consistent multi-probe reaction analysis but does not fully eliminate the spectroscopic-factor puzzle.

status_evidence.title: Explanation for spectroscopic factor quenching in knockout reactions
status_evidence.snippet: Proposes a core screening effect due to a finite-sized probe to explain the systematic quenching of spectroscopic factors.
status_evidence.claim: A 2025 proposal offers a partial mechanistic explanation, indicating the problem is still being actively investigated.

status_evidence.title: Erratum: New Perspectives on Spectroscopic Factor Quenching from Reactions
status_evidence.snippet: Erratum to the 2023 PRL on spectroscopic factor quenching.
status_evidence.claim: The reaction-model treatment of spectroscopic-factor extractions continues to be refined and corrected.
